newsitem.title: FRANCE: France keeps up pressure on U.S. over Zaire. [CORRECTED 14:57 GMT]
newsitem.headline: France keeps up pressure on U.S. over Zaire. [CORRECTED 14:57 GMT]

text.p: France stepped up criticism of the United States on Tuesday for dragging its feet over joining a multinational force to secure urgent relief for starving refugees in eastern Zaire.

The latest blast by Defence Minister Charles Millon came on the eve of a visit to Paris by U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who is expected to face strong pressure to approve a U.N. mandate for an emergency humanitarian operation in Zaire and U.S. participation in the proposed force.
"Intervening is urgent and procrastination by some countries is intolerable," Defence Minister Charles Millon told Europe 1 radio. "The United States must not drag its feet any longer."
France, Spain, Mali and South Africa have pledged troops to an international force to help hundreds of thousands of refugees at risk of dying of hunger and thirst in eastern Zaire.

Canada has offered to lead the force. But the United Nations is still waiting to hear from the United States and Britain, with Washington expected to give its answer on troops for the Central African region before the end of the week.

Washington is edging towards involvement but has sought additional information on the role of the force, command lines and an "exit scenario" while pursuing political solutions to pacify eastern Zaire.

Christopher was due to arrive on Tuesday night and hold talks with Foreign Minister Herve de Charette on Wednesday before attending an international conference on Bosnia in the French capital on Thursday, U.S. officials said.
The U.N. Security Council on Saturday asked members to lay the groundwork for such a force but held off authorising it until its aims and participation were clear.

"It is shocking that the international community is unable to face a humanitarian challenge that will shortly bring about a disaster," Millon said. "I hope that we will be able to give an answer in the coming hours. Restoring a small hope to the refugees is urgent."
More than a million Hutu refugees have been displaced by four weeks of fighting in which rival Tutsi rebels have seized control of a strip of Zaire bordering on Rwanda and Burundi.

Paris insists that a relief force of about 5,000 men, approved by Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko, who is convalescing in France after prostate cancer treatment, must include U.S. and African troops as well as European contingents.

Rwanda and the Rwandan-backed Tutsi rebels have voiced opposition to French military involvement, accusing Paris of backing the former Hutu rulers in the central African state, overthrown in 1994 (corrects year) after a massacre of Tutsis.
Millon said 1,000 French soldiers despatched from France or bases in Africa could be in eastern Zaire within 48 hours if the United Nations reach an agreement on the multinational force.

On Monday, a contingent of 143 French troops arrived in Brazzaville, capital of the neighbouring Congo just across the Zaire River from Kinshasa, the Zairean capital, but their mission was not disclosed.
Millon said military commands in unspecified countries were already making plans to share out operational tasks for their troops in the region.

Former French humanitarian action minister Bernard Kouchner issued an appeal signed by 22 fellow European Parliament members from across the political spectrum, addressed to the U.S. government and the U.N. Security Council.
"We know that each extra hour of waiting in Zaire means the inevitable death of thousands of starving and exhausted men, women and children," the appeal said.

"The Security Council vote is awaiting the gracious will of the United States. Its government has shown its determination in the past to help civilians in distress. Its hesitation today offends human consciences," it said.
